text: HAVE WE NOT opened up thy heart,<sup foot_note=94001>1</sup>
and lifted from thee the burden
that had weighed so heavily on thy back?<sup foot_note=94002>2</sup>

foot_notes.94002: I.e., "the burden of thy past sins, which are now forgiven" (Tabari, on the authority of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd). In the case of Muhammad, this relates apparently to mistakes committed before his call to prophethood (ibid.), and is obviously an echo of 93:7—'Has He not found thee lost on thy way, and guided thee?"

text: And [have We not] raised thee high in dignity?<sup foot_note=94003>3</sup>

foot_notes.94003: Or: "raised high thy renown". The primary meaning of the term dhikr is "reminder" or "remembrance"; and, secondarily, "that by which something [or "someone"] is remembered", i.e., with praise: hence, it signifies "fame" or "renown", and, tropically—as in the present context—"eminence" or "dignity".

text: And, behold, with every hardship comes ease:
verily, with every hardship comes ease!
Hence, when thou art freed [from distress], remain steadfast,
and unto thy Sustainer turn with love.
